newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-FORECAST-Pasminco half net to slide.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-FORECAST-Pasminco half net to slide.

text.p: Last year's dull metal prices and stronger Australian dollar are expected to have cut Pasminco Ltd's profits for the six months to December 31 by more than a third against those of a year ago, analysts said.
Pasminco, which reports its first-half results on Wednesday, has warned of difficult times for fiscal 1996/97 (July/June).
The world's largest zinc producer was, on average, seen posting a first-half net profit before abnormals of A$13 million, down 36 percent on the December 1995 half.
"It's going to be tough, currency is the killer," said one Sydney-based analyst who declined to be named.
Pasminco, like many Australian miners, had its predominantly export-based earnings hammered by a US$0.05 hike in the local currency to an average of US$0.79 for the December half.
The company said in October its after-tax profits shed A$7.5 million for every one cent rise in the Australian dollar.
Analysts said Pasminco's prospects were given little assistance by the price of zinc, its main earner, which eked out a US$3.00 a tonne gain to average US$1,043 over the six months.
The company's zinc smelters also suffered a slight fall in total ouput for the period to 265,888 tonnes while mine production rose a touch.

"Production has been at a reasonable level. They've had problems with maintenance but they've all been scheduled though. Mines probably haven't performed as well as they should," said Bell Commodities base metals analyst Bruce Preston.
Analysts forecast stable production costs in the first half but said the higher local dollar would have pushed Pasminco's break-even zinc price over the US$900 a tonne it reported in October.
"In an actual operational sense in just Australian dollar terms, costs will probably be around flat half on half," said Will Corkill, analyst at Macquarie Equities.
"I would suggest that they're struggling to maintain US$900 per tonne (break even price) in zinc because the currency's been against them," said the Sydney analyst.

But analysts said the company's second half would shine on the back of a recent surge in world zinc prices to levels not seen since January 1995. Nickel ended Thursday's London Metal Exchange dealings at US$1,216 a tonne.
They said the result also would be boosted by a slide in the Australian dollar from last year's US$0.82 peak to its current level of roughly US$0.77.
"The second half will be a hell of a lot better. We're going for A$36 million to A$40 million (net profit) for the second half," Corkill said.
Another analyst said: "They should make about A$30 million in the second half. It will be marginally better I think providing (prices) remain where they are or better."
Pasminco made a net profit of A$20.6 million in the second half of 1995/96. -- Melbourne bureau 61-3 9286-1435
